title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Chylomicrons. In the smooth ER, fatty acids and monoglycerides re-form triglycerides, packed with cholesterol, phospholipids and apoproteins.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: GLUT2. All monosaccharides leave the enterocyte on the basolateral side by facilitated diffusion.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: GLUT5. Fructose enters by facilitated diffusion, without sodium.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Lymphatic route. Chylomicrons are too large for capillaries: they enter lacteals and reach blood through the thoracic duct.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Micelles. Bile salts carry lipolysis products to the brush border, where they diffuse into the cell.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Portal circulation. Sugars and amino acids go through the portal vein to the liver.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: SGLT1. Secondary active transport: glucose and galactose enter with Na⁺, driven by the basolateral Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase.

title: Three levels of surface amplification?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Three levels of surface amplification?
body.back: Circular folds, villi, microvilli → ~200 m².

title: Sugar transporters?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Sugar transporters?
body.back: SGLT1 (glucose, galactose + Na⁺), GLUT5 (fructose), GLUT2 (exit).

title: Four steps of fat absorption?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Four steps of fat absorption?
body.back: Lipolysis, micelles, re-esterification, chylomicrons into lymph.

title: B12 absorption pathway?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: B12 absorption pathway?
body.back: R protein in stomach → freed by pancreatic proteases → intrinsic factor → terminal ileum.

title: What does the ileum specifically absorb?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What does the ileum specifically absorb?
body.back: Vitamin B12 and bile salts.

title: Daily fluid load of the gut?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Daily fluid load of the gut?
body.back: ~10-11 L absorbed; 50-200 mL in stool.

title: Calcium and iron absorption site?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Calcium and iron absorption site?
body.back: Both in the duodenum; calcium needs vitamin D.

title: Maldigestion vs malabsorption?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Maldigestion vs malabsorption?
body.back: Maldigestion: enzyme or bile deficit. Malabsorption: mucosal damage or lost surface.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Voluntary decision. If appropriate, cortical centres allow defecation; otherwise the external sphincter and puborectalis hold and the rectum adapts.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Rectal distension. Stool entering the rectum stretches its wall; signals go through the pelvic nerves to the brain.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Expulsion. Rectal contraction, raised intra-abdominal pressure (Valsalva) and pelvic floor descent evacuate the rectum.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Recto-anal excitatory reflex. Reflex contraction of the external sphincter guards continence while the internal sphincter is relaxed.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Recto-anal inhibitory reflex. Transient relaxation of the internal anal sphincter lets the anal canal 'sample' contents; absent in Hirschsprung disease.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Sphincter and puborectalis relaxation. Voluntary relaxation via the pudendal nerve (S2-S4); the puborectalis relaxes and the anorectal angle straightens.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Sampling. The sensitive anal canal distinguishes gas, liquid and solid, and the desire to defecate is felt.

title: IAS vs EAS?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: IAS vs EAS?
body.back: IAS: smooth, involuntary, ~70% resting tone. EAS: striated, voluntary, pudendal nerve.

title: Role of puborectalis?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Role of puborectalis?
body.back: Sling keeping the anorectal angle ~80-90°; relaxes during defecation.

title: RAIR vs RAER?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: RAIR vs RAER?
body.back: RAIR: IAS relaxes (sampling). RAER: EAS contracts (guarding).

title: Four continence mechanisms?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Four continence mechanisms?
body.back: Compliance, sphincter resistance, initial continence, rectal adaptation.

title: Steps of expulsion?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Steps of expulsion?
body.back: Rectal contraction, IAS/EAS/puborectalis relaxation, Valsalva, pelvic floor descent.

title: Anorectal tests?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Anorectal tests?
body.back: Manometry, endoanal ultrasound, defecography, endoscopy.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Combined effect. Greater filling plus greater contractility: EDV 165 mL − ESV 35 mL = SV 130 mL, as during exercise.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Cardiac output. Stroke volume times heart rate: about 5 L/min at rest, rising to 20-30 L/min during exercise.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Frank-Starling mechanism. More venous return stretches the fibres (higher preload, EDV 165 mL); they contract more strongly and eject more (SV 100 mL) with the same ESV.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Resting stroke volume. End-diastolic volume about 135 mL minus end-systolic volume about 65 mL gives a stroke volume of about 70 mL, an ejection fraction near 52%.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Sympathetic stimulation. Noradrenaline on β1 receptors increases contractility, so the ventricle empties more (ESV 35 mL) from the same EDV: SV 100 mL.

title: Systole and diastole?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Systole and diastole?
body.back: Systole: ventricular contraction and ejection. Diastole: relaxation and filling.

title: Heart sounds?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Heart sounds?
body.back: S1: closure of mitral and tricuspid valves. S2: closure of aortic and pulmonary valves.

title: Incompetent vs stenotic valve?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Incompetent vs stenotic valve?
body.back: Incompetent: fails to close (leak, swishing). Stenotic: fails to open fully (high-pitched sound, click).

title: When is each murmur heard?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: When is each murmur heard?
body.back: Systolic: mitral/tricuspid regurgitation, aortic/pulmonary stenosis. Diastolic: mitral stenosis, aortic regurgitation.

title: Cardiac output formula and values?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Cardiac output formula and values?
body.back: CO = HR × SV; ~5 L/min at rest, 20-30 L/min in exercise.

title: Starling's law?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Starling's law?
body.back: Greater preload (fibre stretch from venous return, EDV) → stronger contraction → larger SV, up to an optimum.

title: Extrinsic control of SV?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Extrinsic control of SV?
body.back: Sympathetic NE on β1 and thyroid hormones increase contractility, lowering ESV.

title: Ejection fraction?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Ejection fraction?
body.back: EF = SV / EDV; normal 50-75%; rises with contractility.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Systemic circulation. High-pressure loop to all organs, holding about 84% of total blood volume; returns through the venae cavae.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Left heart. Receives oxygenated blood from the four pulmonary veins and pumps it into the aorta at high pressure (about 120/80 mmHg).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Pulmonary circulation. Low-pressure loop: pulmonary arteries carry oxygen-poor blood to the lungs and pulmonary veins bring oxygenated blood back to the left atrium.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Flow, pressure, resistance. Flow equals driving pressure over resistance; by Poiseuille, resistance rises with viscosity and length and falls with the fourth power of radius.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Right heart. Receives deoxygenated blood from the venae cavae and pumps it into the pulmonary arteries.

title: Three components of the cardiovascular system?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Three components of the cardiovascular system?
body.back: Heart (pump), vessels (pipes), blood (fluid).

title: Pulmonary vs systemic loop?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Pulmonary vs systemic loop?
body.back: Pulmonary: RV → lungs → LA (low pressure). Systemic: LV → organs → RA (high pressure, 84% of volume).

title: Exception to 'arteries carry oxygenated blood'?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Exception to 'arteries carry oxygenated blood'?
body.back: Pulmonary arteries carry deoxygenated blood; pulmonary veins carry oxygenated blood.

title: Relation between flow, pressure and resistance?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Relation between flow, pressure and resistance?
body.back: Q = ΔP / R.

title: Poiseuille's law?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Poiseuille's law?
body.back: R = 8ηL / πr⁴: viscosity, length, radius to the fourth power.

title: Why are arterioles key?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Why are arterioles key?
body.back: Small muscular vessels whose radius changes control resistance and flow distribution.

title: What is EDRF?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is EDRF?
body.back: Nitric oxide made by endothelial NO synthase in response to shear stress, ACh, ADP; relaxes smooth muscle.

title: Furchgott's experiment?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Furchgott's experiment?
body.back: ACh relaxes an aortic ring with endothelium but constricts it without; revealed EDRF (NO).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Gastrocolic reflex. Gastric distension after a meal increases colonic motor activity via vagal and spinal afferents, modulated by gastrin.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Mass movements (HAPCs). Mass movements, a few times a day, pushing stool from the ascending colon to the rectosigmoid.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Haustral contractions. Non-propulsive ring contractions of the proximal colon that mix contents, maximise water absorption and keep contact with the microbiota.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Propulsive contractions. Low- to medium-amplitude peristalsis in the transverse and descending colon, moving stool slowly towards the sigmoid.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Retrograde contractions. Start at the ascending-transverse junction and run back towards the caecum, slowing transit and preventing premature rectal filling.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Urge. Mass movements filling the rectum precede the sensation of urgency and defecation.

title: Taeniae coli and haustra?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Taeniae coli and haustra?
body.back: Three longitudinal muscle bands; sacculations between them.

title: Four colonic motor patterns?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Four colonic motor patterns?
body.back: Haustral, propulsive, retrograde, HAPCs (mass movements).

title: Gastrocolic reflex?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Gastrocolic reflex?
body.back: Meal distends stomach → increased colonic motility.

title: Colonic pacemaker?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Colonic pacemaker?
body.back: Interstitial cells of Cajal, 2-6/min.

title: Extrinsic nerves of the colon?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Extrinsic nerves of the colon?
body.back: Parasympathetic (vagus, S2-S4): excitatory. Sympathetic (T10-L2): inhibitory.

title: Hirschsprung disease?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Hirschsprung disease?
body.back: Aganglionic distal bowel; delayed meconium; rectal biopsy.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: P wave. Atrial depolarisation spreading from the SA node; small because the atrial wall is thin; normally 0.08-0.10 s and under 2.5 mm.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: PR interval. Atrioventricular conduction time from the start of P to the start of QRS, 0.12-0.20 s; longer suggests first-degree AV block.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: QRS complex. Ventricular depolarisation starting in the left side of the septum; Q is the first negative, R the first positive and S the next negative deflection.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: QT interval. From the start of QRS to the end of T, 0.35-0.44 s: the whole of ventricular depolarisation and repolarisation.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: ST segment. Isoelectric while the ventricles are fully depolarised; elevation can signal myocardial ischaemia or injury.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: T wave. Ventricular repolarisation; normally positive except in aVR, V1, V2 and sometimes DIII.

title: Two types of cardiac tissue?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Two types of cardiac tissue?
body.back: Nodal tissue (SA, AV, His, Purkinje: generates and conducts) and myocardium (contracts).

title: Phases of the myocardial action potential?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Phases of the myocardial action potential?
body.back: 0: Na⁺ in; 1: early repolarisation; 2: plateau; 3: K⁺ out; 4: rest (−90 mV).

title: Dipole rule for deflections?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Dipole rule for deflections?
body.back: Depolarisation moving towards the electrode → positive; moving away → negative; no moving front → isoelectric.

title: Paper speed and gain?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Paper speed and gain?
body.back: 25 mm/s (1 mm = 0.04 s); 10 mm per mV (1 mm = 0.1 mV).

title: The 12 leads?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: The 12 leads?
body.back: Limb: DI, DII, DIII, aVR, aVL, aVF (frontal). Chest: V1-V6 (horizontal).

title: Normal intervals?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Normal intervals?

title: Signs of LVH?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Signs of LVH?
body.back: R(DI) + S(DIII) ≥ 30 mm or R(V5/V6) + S(V1/V2) ≥ 35 mm; left axis deviation.

title: ECG territories?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: ECG territories?
body.back: Inferior: DII, DIII, aVF. Anteroseptal: V1-V3. Anterior: V1-V5. Apical: V3-V4. Lateral: DI, aVL, V5, V6.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Carrier proteins. TBG, CBG, SHBG and albumin carry lipophilic hormones, prolonging half-life and buffering the free, active fraction.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Rapid responses. Second messengers (cAMP, IP₃/Ca²⁺, DAG) change enzyme activity within seconds to minutes.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Membrane receptors. G protein-coupled receptors (Gs, Gi, Gq), receptor tyrosine kinases (insulin, IGF-1) and cytokine receptors using JAK/STAT (GH, prolactin).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Nuclear receptors. Ligand-regulated transcription factors: steroid receptors move from cytosol to nucleus; the thyroid receptor sits on DNA and switches from repressor to activator.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Water-soluble hormones. Peptides (insulin, GH, ACTH) and catecholamines cannot cross the membrane; they are stored in granules and released by Ca²⁺-dependent exocytosis.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Genomic responses. Changes in gene transcription and protein synthesis, taking hours to days.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Lipid-soluble hormones. Steroids are made from cholesterol on demand; thyroid hormone is a tyrosine derivative transported into the cell.

title: Endocrine vs exocrine?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Endocrine vs exocrine?
body.back: Endocrine: ductless, blood. Exocrine: ducts, surfaces.

title: Four modes of hormone signalling?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Four modes of hormone signalling?
body.back: Endocrine, paracrine, autocrine, intracrine.

title: Receptor location by class?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Receptor location by class?
body.back: Peptides and catecholamines: membrane. Steroids and thyroid hormone: intracellular.

title: GPCR pathways?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: GPCR pathways?
body.back: Gs ↑ cAMP (ACTH, TSH, LH, FSH); Gi ↓ cAMP (dopamine); Gq IP₃/Ca²⁺ (TRH, GnRH).

title: RTK vs JAK/STAT?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: RTK vs JAK/STAT?
body.back: RTK has intrinsic kinase (insulin, IGF-1). Cytokine receptor uses JAK2 (GH, prolactin).

title: Why measure free hormone?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Why measure free hormone?
body.back: Only free hormone is active; binding proteins change totals.

title: Three feedback loops?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Three feedback loops?
body.back: Long (target → pituitary/hypothalamus), short (pituitary → hypothalamus), ultra-short (self).

title: Primary vs secondary failure pattern?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Primary vs secondary failure pattern?
body.back: Primary: tropic ↑, target ↓. Secondary: both ↓.

title: Tachyphylaxis vs tolerance?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Tachyphylaxis vs tolerance?
body.back: Tachyphylaxis: fast, not overcome by dose. Tolerance: slow, partly overcome.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Antral grinding. Peristaltic waves driven by slow waves grind solids; retropulsion against a closing pylorus mixes and breaks them.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Duodenal brake. Fat, acid and hyperosmolar chyme release CCK, secretin and GIP, which slow emptying (enterogastrones).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Receptive relaxation. A vagovagal reflex (NO, VIP) lets the fundus relax as food arrives, so volume rises with little pressure rise.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Migrating motor complex. Every 80-120 min in fasting, phase III sweeps indigestible solids through the pylorus; motilin triggers it.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Pyloric sieving. Only particles under about 1-2 mm pass during feeding, at about 2-3 kcal per minute.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Proximal tone. Slow tonic contraction of the proximal stomach pushes liquids out: liquid emptying depends on this pressure gradient.

title: Who paces the stomach?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Who paces the stomach?
body.back: Interstitial cells of Cajal: slow waves about 3/min.

title: What is the MMC?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is the MMC?
body.back: Fasting cycle (80-120 min); phase III sweeps residue; triggered by motilin.

title: Receptive relaxation?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Receptive relaxation?
body.back: Vagovagal relaxation of the fundus on swallowing (NO, VIP).

title: Liquids vs solids emptying?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Liquids vs solids emptying?
body.back: Liquids: proximal tone, exponential. Solids: lag phase, antral grinding, linear.

title: Pyloric particle size?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Pyloric particle size?
body.back: About 1-2 mm during feeding.

title: Enterogastrones?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Enterogastrones?
body.back: Secretin, CCK, GIP: slow emptying.

title: Causes of gastroparesis?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Causes of gastroparesis?
body.back: Diabetes, scleroderma, Parkinson's, amyloidosis, drugs, surgery.

title: Prokinetic drugs?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Prokinetic drugs?
body.back: Metoclopramide, domperidone (D2 antagonists); erythromycin (motilin agonist).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Somatostatin. When antral pH falls below about 3, D cells release somatostatin, which inhibits gastrin release: negative feedback.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Histamine. Paracrine release from ECL cells, acting on H2 receptors (cAMP); blocked by cimetidine and other H2 antagonists.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Gastrin. Released by antral G cells in response to GRP (vagus), distension and amino acids; acts on CCK2 receptors of parietal and ECL cells.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Secretion. HCl at about 150-160 mM (pH 1-2) and intrinsic factor, needed for vitamin B12 absorption in the ileum.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Parietal cell. The H⁺/K⁺ ATPase (proton pump) pumps H⁺ out in exchange for K⁺; Cl⁻ follows through apical channels. Blocked by omeprazole.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Acetylcholine. Vagal and enteric neurons release ACh onto M3 receptors of the parietal cell (Ca²⁺ pathway); atropine blocks it.

title: Cells of gastric glands and their products?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Cells of gastric glands and their products?
body.back: Parietal: HCl, IF. Chief: pepsinogen, lipase. G: gastrin. D: somatostatin. ECL: histamine. Mucous: mucus.

title: How is H⁺ produced?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: How is H⁺ produced?
body.back: Carbonic anhydrase: CO₂ + H₂O → H⁺ + HCO₃⁻; H⁺/K⁺ ATPase pumps H⁺ out.

title: What is the alkaline tide?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is the alkaline tide?
body.back: HCO₃⁻ exchanged for Cl⁻ enters the blood during acid secretion.

title: Three stimulants of the parietal cell?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Three stimulants of the parietal cell?
body.back: ACh (M3), gastrin (CCK2), histamine (H2); they potentiate.

title: Negative feedback on acid?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Negative feedback on acid?
body.back: Antral pH < 3 → D cells release somatostatin → less gastrin.

title: Phases of gastric secretion?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Phases of gastric secretion?
body.back: Cephalic ~30%, gastric ~60%, intestinal (inhibitory: secretin, GIP, somatostatin).

title: Role of intrinsic factor?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Role of intrinsic factor?
body.back: Binds B12 for absorption in the terminal ileum.

title: Zollinger-Ellison?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Zollinger-Ellison?
body.back: Gastrinoma → massive acid → multiple ulcers.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Absorption. Transfer of nutrients, water and electrolytes across the mucosa, mainly in the small intestine.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Digestion. Mechanical and chemical breakdown of carbohydrates, proteins and fats into absorbable units.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Elimination. The colon absorbs water and stores faeces until defecation.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Regulation. The enteric nervous system, autonomic nerves and hormones (gastrin, CCK, secretin, GIP, motilin) coordinate everything.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Motility. Smooth muscle mixes food with secretions and moves it aborally: peristalsis, segmentation, gastric grinding.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Secretion. Glands add water, electrolytes, enzymes, acid, mucus and bile: several litres a day, mostly reabsorbed.

title: Four functions of the gut?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Four functions of the gut?
body.back: Motility, secretion, digestion, absorption (then elimination).

title: Myenteric vs submucosal plexus?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Myenteric vs submucosal plexus?
body.back: Myenteric (Auerbach): motility. Submucosal (Meissner): secretion and blood flow.

title: Where is most absorption?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Where is most absorption?
body.back: Small intestine.

title: Does bile contain enzymes?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Does bile contain enzymes?
body.back: No: bile salts emulsify fat.

title: Three phases of digestive control?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Three phases of digestive control?
body.back: Cephalic, gastric, intestinal.

title: Five classic GI hormones?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Five classic GI hormones?
body.back: Gastrin, CCK, secretin, GIP, motilin.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Autonomic control. Sympathetic noradrenaline on β1 receptors speeds and strengthens the heart; vagal acetylcholine on muscarinic receptors slows the nodes.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Atrioventricular node. Slows conduction by about 0.1 s so the atria finish emptying before the ventricles contract; can pace at about 50/min.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Bundle of His and branches. The only electrical path through the fibrous skeleton from atria to ventricles, dividing into right and left bundle branches along the septum.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Purkinje fibres. Fast conducting fibres spreading excitation from the apex upward through the ventricles and to the papillary muscles; intrinsic rate about 30/min.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Sinoatrial node. Dominant pacemaker in the right atrium, firing about 70 times a minute thanks to its spontaneous pacemaker potential.

title: Three layers of the heart wall?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Three layers of the heart wall?
body.back: Epicardium (visceral pericardium), myocardium (muscle), endocardium (endothelium).

title: Components of the conducting system?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Components of the conducting system?
body.back: SA node, internodal pathways, AV node, bundle of His, bundle branches, Purkinje fibres.

title: Why the AV nodal delay?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Why the AV nodal delay?
body.back: About 0.1 s lets the atria contract and finish filling the ventricles.

title: Intrinsic pacemaker rates?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Intrinsic pacemaker rates?
body.back: SA ~70/min, AV ~50/min, Purkinje ~30/min.

title: Ionic basis of the pacemaker potential?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Ionic basis of the pacemaker potential?
body.back: Funny current I_f (Na⁺ in, activated by hyperpolarisation) and T-type Ca²⁺ channels.

title: Autonomic effects on the heart?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Autonomic effects on the heart?
body.back: Sympathetic NE/adrenaline on β1: ↑ rate and contractility. Vagal ACh on muscarinic: ↓ rate.

title: Endocrine role of the heart?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Endocrine role of the heart?
body.back: Atrial cells secrete ANP when stretched → Na⁺ excretion.

title: Atrial vs ventricular fibrillation?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Atrial vs ventricular fibrillation?
body.back: Atrial: poor filling, clots, stroke risk. Ventricular: no output, cardiac arrest → defibrillation.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Anterior pituitary. Glandular lobe secreting six main hormones: TSH, FSH, LH (glycoproteins), ACTH (POMC), GH and prolactin.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Direct release. The posterior lobe hormones enter systemic blood by exocytosis from nerve endings.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Dopamine. The only inhibitory control dominant over a pituitary hormone: cutting the stalk raises prolactin.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Hypophysiotropic neurons. Parvocellular PVN (CRH, TRH), arcuate (GHRH, dopamine), preoptic area (GnRH), PVN (somatostatin).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Hypophyseal portal system. Releasing and inhibiting hormones are secreted at the median eminence and carried to the anterior lobe.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Posterior pituitary. Neural lobe: axon terminals store and release ADH and oxytocin.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Magnocellular neurons. Cell bodies in the supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei make ADH and oxytocin with their neurophysins.

title: Where are ADH and oxytocin made?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Where are ADH and oxytocin made?
body.back: Supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei; released from the posterior pituitary.

title: Stimuli for ADH?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Stimuli for ADH?
body.back: ↑ osmolality, ↓ volume/pressure, angiotensin II, pain, nausea. Inhibited by alcohol.

title: ADH receptors?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: ADH receptors?
body.back: V2 (Gs): aquaporin-2. V1A (Gq): vasoconstriction, glycogenolysis. V1B: ACTH.

title: Central vs nephrogenic DI?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Central vs nephrogenic DI?
body.back: Central: no ADH. Nephrogenic: kidney resistant (V2 mutation, lithium, low K⁺).

title: SIADH findings?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: SIADH findings?
body.back: Concentrated urine, dilutional hyponatraemia.

title: Hypothalamic controllers of the anterior pituitary?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Hypothalamic controllers of the anterior pituitary?
body.back: CRH, TRH, GHRH, somatostatin, GnRH, dopamine.

title: GH direct vs indirect effects?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: GH direct vs indirect effects?
body.back: Direct: lipolysis, diabetogenic, protein synthesis. Indirect via IGF-1: skeletal growth.

title: Control of prolactin?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Control of prolactin?
body.back: Dopamine (D2) inhibits; TRH stimulates.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Expiratory reserve volume. The extra air that can be forced out after a normal tidal expiration.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Functional residual capacity. The gas left after a normal expiration: ERV + RV; increased by air trapping in obstructive disease.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Inspiratory capacity. The volume that can be inspired from the end of a normal expiration: IRV + VT.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Inspiratory reserve volume. The extra air that can be forced in after a normal tidal inspiration.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Residual volume. The air left in the lungs after a maximal expiration; it cannot be measured by simple spirometry.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Total lung capacity. All the gas in the lungs after a maximal inspiration: VC + RV.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Vital capacity. The maximal volume exhaled after a maximal inspiration: IRV + VT + ERV.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Tidal volume. The air breathed in or out in quiet breathing, about 500 mL.

title: Four lung volumes?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Four lung volumes?
body.back: Tidal volume, inspiratory reserve volume, expiratory reserve volume, residual volume.

title: Vital capacity?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Vital capacity?
body.back: IRV + VT + ERV: maximal expiration after maximal inspiration.

title: Total lung capacity?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Total lung capacity?
body.back: VC + RV (≈ 6 L).

title: FRC and IC?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: FRC and IC?
body.back: FRC = ERV + RV (after normal expiration). IC = IRV + VT.

title: Which volume needs more than spirometry?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Which volume needs more than spirometry?
body.back: Residual volume (and thus FRC, TLC).

title: Pressures in inspiration?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Pressures in inspiration?
body.back: Diaphragm contracts → pleural pressure falls → alveolar pressure below atmospheric → inflow.

title: Air trapping?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Air trapping?
body.back: In obstruction, airways close early: RV and FRC rise, lungs hyperinflate.

title: COPD facts?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: COPD facts?
body.back: Chronic bronchitis + emphysema; ~80% smoking; ~3.2 million deaths worldwide (2015).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Gut-brain axis. Microbial metabolites and neurotransmitters influence mood, stress (HPA axis) and neurological disease.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Dysbiosis. Imbalance linked to IBD, obesity, type 2 diabetes and recurrent Clostridioides difficile infection.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Immune role. Maturation of GALT and balance of pro- and anti-inflammatory cytokines; tolerance to commensals.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Microbiota. Bacteria (95%), viruses, fungi, archaea and protozoa; density rises from stomach to colon.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Metabolic role. Fermentation of fibre into acetate, propionate and butyrate; synthesis of vitamin K and B vitamins; bile acid transformation.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Colonisation resistance. Competition for nutrients and sites, bacteriocins and organic acids, and mucus support keep pathogens out.

title: Main bacterial phyla?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Main bacterial phyla?
body.back: Firmicutes, Bacteroidetes, Actinobacteria, Proteobacteria, Verrucomicrobia.

title: Three SCFAs and roles?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Three SCFAs and roles?
body.back: Acetate (energy), propionate (liver gluconeogenesis), butyrate (colonocytes).

title: Five functions of microbiota?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Five functions of microbiota?
body.back: Metabolism, protection, immunity, gut-brain axis, energy balance.

title: Probiotic vs prebiotic vs synbiotic?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Probiotic vs prebiotic vs synbiotic?
body.back: Live organisms; non-digestible fibre; both together.

title: FMT indication?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: FMT indication?
body.back: Recurrent C. difficile infection (~90% success).

title: Distribution along the gut?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Distribution along the gut?
body.back: Low in stomach/duodenum, higher in ileum, highest in colon.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Acinar cells. Secrete a primary fluid similar to plasma (isotonic), plus amylase, lipase and mucins.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Aldosterone. Acts on the ducts like on the kidney: more Na⁺ reabsorption and K⁺ secretion.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Duct modification. Ducts reabsorb Na⁺ and Cl⁻ and secrete K⁺ and HCO₃⁻; the ducts are poorly permeable to water.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Hypotonic saliva. Because salt is removed without water, final saliva is hypotonic; at high flow it has less time to be modified.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Parasympathetic control. The main stimulus (CN VII and IX, acetylcholine): large volumes of watery saliva.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Sympathetic control. Produces a smaller volume of viscous, protein-rich saliva.

title: Saliva composition?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Saliva composition?
body.back: 99.5% water; electrolytes, amylase, lingual lipase, mucins, lysozyme, IgA, lactoferrin.

title: Two-stage secretion?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Two-stage secretion?
body.back: Acini: isotonic fluid. Ducts: reabsorb Na⁺/Cl⁻, secrete K⁺/HCO₃⁻ → hypotonic.

title: Autonomic control of saliva?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Autonomic control of saliva?
body.back: Parasympathetic: large watery volume. Sympathetic: small viscous volume.

title: Muscles of mastication and nerve?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Muscles of mastication and nerve?
body.back: Masseter, temporalis, medial and lateral pterygoids; V3.

title: Three phases of swallowing?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Three phases of swallowing?
body.back: Oral (voluntary), pharyngeal (reflex), oesophageal (peristalsis).

title: What is Zenker's diverticulum?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is Zenker's diverticulum?
body.back: A pharyngeal pouch above the UES causing regurgitation.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Duodenal acidity. When duodenal pH falls below about 4.5, S cells release secretin.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Acinar cells. Store enzymes as inactive zymogens in granules; lipase and amylase are secreted active.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Cholecystokinin. Stimulates acinar enzyme secretion (with the vagus) and contracts the gallbladder.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Ductal secretion. Duct cells secrete HCO₃⁻ via CFTR and the Cl⁻/HCO₃⁻ exchanger; defective CFTR in cystic fibrosis gives thick secretions.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Activation cascade. Enterokinase on the duodenal brush border activates trypsinogen; trypsin then activates all the other zymogens.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Nutrients. Fatty acids and amino acids in the duodenum are the stimulus for CCK release.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Secretin. The main stimulus of water and bicarbonate secretion by the duct cells.

title: Acinar vs duct cells?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Acinar vs duct cells?
body.back: Acinar: enzymes (zymogens). Duct: water and HCO₃⁻.

title: Secretin vs CCK?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Secretin vs CCK?
body.back: Secretin (acid): bicarbonate. CCK (fat, amino acids): enzymes and gallbladder contraction.

title: How are proteases activated?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: How are proteases activated?
body.back: Enterokinase activates trypsinogen → trypsin, which activates the others.

title: Enzymes secreted active?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Enzymes secreted active?
body.back: Lipase and amylase.

title: Protection from autodigestion?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Protection from autodigestion?
body.back: Zymogens, trypsin inhibitors (SPINK1/PSTI, Kunitz).

title: Diagnosis of acute pancreatitis?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Diagnosis of acute pancreatitis?
body.back: Typical pain + lipase > 3 × normal (or imaging).

title: Consequences of chronic pancreatitis?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Consequences of chronic pancreatitis?
body.back: Steatorrhoea, calcifications, diabetes.

title: Test for exocrine insufficiency?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Test for exocrine insufficiency?
body.back: Faecal elastase (< 200 µg/g).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Bronchoconstriction. Low local PCO₂ constricts the bronchioles supplying that region, reducing wasted ventilation.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction. Pulmonary arterioles constrict in response to low alveolar PO₂, via oxygen-sensitive K⁺ channels and voltage-gated Ca²⁺ entry in smooth muscle; systemic arteries do the opposite.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Low alveolar CO₂. An alveolus that is poorly perfused (e.g. embolism) receives little CO₂, so its PCO₂ falls.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Low alveolar oxygen. An alveolus that is poorly ventilated (mucus, pneumonia, atelectasis) has a low PO₂.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Matching. Air goes where blood is: ventilation adjusted to perfusion, the counterpart of HPV.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Redistribution of blood. Perfusion shifts to well-ventilated regions, optimising V/Q and arterial oxygenation.

title: What is HPV?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is HPV?
body.back: Constriction of pulmonary arterioles in response to low alveolar PO₂.

title: Pulmonary vs systemic response to hypoxia?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Pulmonary vs systemic response to hypoxia?
body.back: Pulmonary vessels constrict; systemic vessels dilate.

title: Mechanism of HPV?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Mechanism of HPV?
body.back: Hypoxia closes O₂-sensitive K⁺ channels → depolarisation → voltage-gated Ca²⁺ entry → contraction.

title: Is HPV good or bad?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Is HPV good or bad?
body.back: Local: good (optimises V/Q). Global chronic hypoxia: bad (pulmonary hypertension).

title: Role of HPV in the fetus?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Role of HPV in the fetus?
body.back: Keeps pulmonary resistance high so blood bypasses the lungs via foramen ovale and ductus.

title: Perfusion adjusted to ventilation?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Perfusion adjusted to ventilation?
body.back: Low airflow → low PO₂ → vasoconstriction; high airflow → vasodilatation.

title: Ventilation adjusted to perfusion?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Ventilation adjusted to perfusion?
body.back: Low blood flow → low PCO₂ → bronchoconstriction; high flow → bronchodilatation.

title: V/Q in asthma vs embolism?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: V/Q in asthma vs embolism?
body.back: Asthma: low V/Q (poorly ventilated, perfused). Embolism: high V/Q (ventilated, unperfused).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Arterial blood. Blood leaving the lungs equilibrates with alveolar gas: PaO₂ about 100 and PaCO₂ about 40 mmHg.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Fick's law of diffusion. Gas transfer is proportional to surface area, solubility and partial pressure difference, and inversely proportional to membrane thickness and (the square root of) molecular weight.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Alveolar gas. Mixing with CO₂ from the blood lowers alveolar PO₂ to about 100 mmHg and raises PCO₂ to about 40 mmHg.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Inspired oxygen pressure. Humidified inspired air: PIO₂ = (barometric pressure − water vapour 47 mmHg) × FIO₂ 0.21 ≈ 150 mmHg at sea level.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Mixed venous blood. Returning from the tissues with PO₂ about 40 and PCO₂ about 45 mmHg; the gradients drive O₂ into and CO₂ out of the blood.

title: Three roles of the lung?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Three roles of the lung?
body.back: Gas exchange, metabolism (e.g. angiotensin conversion), blood reservoir.

title: Fick's law?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Fick's law?
body.back: Diffusion ∝ surface area × solubility × pressure difference / (thickness × √molecular weight).

title: Inspired PO₂ formula?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Inspired PO₂ formula?

title: Normal alveolar and venous pressures?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Normal alveolar and venous pressures?
body.back: PAO₂ ≈ 100, PACO₂ ≈ 40; PvO₂ ≈ 40, PvCO₂ ≈ 45 mmHg.

title: Conducting vs respiratory zone?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Conducting vs respiratory zone?
body.back: Conducting: nose to terminal bronchioles, dead space, conditions air. Respiratory: respiratory bronchioles to alveoli, exchange.

title: VT = ?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: VT = ?

title: Minute vs alveolar ventilation?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Minute vs alveolar ventilation?
body.back: VE = VT × RR = 7.5 L/min; VA = (VT − VD) × RR = 5.25 L/min.

title: Global V/Q?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Global V/Q?
body.back: VA ≈ 5.25 L/min over Q ≈ 4.9 L/min → ≈ 1.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Fasting state. Between meals the small intestine is not at rest: it runs the migrating motor complex.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Fed state. After a meal the MMC stops and the gut switches to mixing and slow propulsion.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Migrating motor complex. A cycle every 90-120 minutes in three phases, started by motilin and suppressed by eating.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Peristalsis. Contraction behind the bolus and relaxation ahead of it, moving chyme aborally.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Phase III. Intense rhythmic contractions that clear undigested residue and bacteria: the housekeeper.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Segmentation. Rhythmic, local ring contractions that mix chyme and increase contact with the mucosa.

title: Length of the small intestine parts?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Length of the small intestine parts?
body.back: Duodenum 25 cm, jejunum ~2 m, ileum ~3 m; total 5-6 m.

title: What is the MMC?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is the MMC?
body.back: Fasting motor cycle every 90-120 min; phases I-III; started by motilin; stopped by eating.

title: Segmentation vs peristalsis?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Segmentation vs peristalsis?
body.back: Segmentation: local mixing. Peristalsis: aboral propulsion.

title: Mediators of peristalsis?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Mediators of peristalsis?
body.back: Contraction: ACh, 5-HT, substance P. Relaxation ahead: NO, VIP.

title: Motility disorders?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Motility disorders?
body.back: Dysmotility (bacterial overgrowth), diarrhoea (fast transit), ileus (no motility).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Coupling. TPO joins iodotyrosines: MIT + DIT → T3; DIT + DIT → T4.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Peripheral activation. Selenium-containing deiodinases convert T4 to the more potent T3 (D1, D2) or inactivate it (D3).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Sodium-iodide symporter. Secondary active transport on the basolateral membrane, driven by the Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase; stimulated by TSH.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Pendrin. A Cl⁻/I⁻ exchanger that moves iodide across the apical membrane into the colloid.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Secretion. TSH triggers endocytosis of thyroglobulin; lysosomes free T4 (mostly) and T3; MIT and DIT are deiodinated and recycled.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Colloid storage. Hormone stays attached to thyroglobulin in the colloid, a 2-3 month supply.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Thyroid peroxidase. Uses H₂O₂ from DUOX to oxidise iodide and attach it to tyrosines of thyroglobulin, forming MIT and DIT.

title: Steps of thyroid hormone synthesis?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Steps of thyroid hormone synthesis?
body.back: NIS uptake, pendrin, TPO oxidation, organification of Tg (MIT/DIT), coupling, storage, endocytosis and release.

title: T3 vs T4?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: T3 vs T4?
body.back: T4 main secreted form; T3 3-5× more potent; T4 → T3 in tissues.

title: Binding proteins?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Binding proteins?
body.back: TBG (most, highest affinity), transthyretin, albumin (highest capacity).

title: Three deiodinases?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Three deiodinases?
body.back: D1 (liver, kidney): T3 and rT3. D2 (brain, pituitary): local T3, feedback. D3: inactivation.

title: Wolff-Chaikoff effect?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Wolff-Chaikoff effect?
body.back: Excess iodide blocks organification; escape by NIS down-regulation.

title: Why TSH is the best test?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Why TSH is the best test?
body.back: Small changes in free T4 cause large inverse changes in TSH.

title: Main effects of thyroid hormone?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Main effects of thyroid hormone?
body.back: ↑ BMR and heat, catabolism, ↑ heart rate and contractility, brain and bone development.

title: Graves vs Hashimoto?
subject: subj:physio1

body.front: Graves vs Hashimoto?
body.back: Graves: TSH-receptor stimulating antibodies, ↑ T4, ↓ TSH. Hashimoto: anti-TPO, ↓ T4, ↑ TSH.
